q: Dimethylamine, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>NH, is classified as a
h: Count the carbon groups bonded directly to the nitrogen.
w: Nitrogen carries two methyl groups and one H, so it is a 2° amine. It has no C=O, so it is not an amide.
x: A primary amine has only one carbon group on N. Here the nitrogen carries two CH<sub>3</sub> groups.
A tertiary amine has three carbon groups on N and no N–H. This nitrogen still has one H.
An amide needs a C=O carbon bonded to the nitrogen. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>NH has no carbonyl group at all.

q: sec-Butylamine, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(NH<sub>2</sub>)CH<sub>3</sub>, is classified as a
h: For amines, count the carbons on the nitrogen, not on the carbon that holds the N.
w: The N is bonded to only one carbon (and two H), so it is a 1° amine. The “sec” describes the alkyl group's carbon, not the amine class; that is the trap behind the 2° answer.
x: The "sec" describes the carbon holding the N, not the nitrogen itself. For amines, count only the carbons bonded directly to N.
A tertiary amine has three carbons on N and no N–H. Look at the –NH<sub>2</sub>: how many carbons does that N actually touch?
A quaternary ammonium ion has four carbons on a positively charged N. This compound is neutral and its N still holds H atoms.

q: What is the common name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>?
h: Name the alkyl group attached to N, then add “amine.”
w: The straight three-carbon group on N is propyl: propylamine. Isopropylamine is (CH3)2CHNH2; propanamide would have a C=O.
x: Isopropyl means the N is on the middle carbon, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH–. In this formula the N sits on the end carbon of a straight chain.
An amide name (-amide) requires a C=O on the carbon bonded to N. This formula has no carbonyl group.
"Di" would mean two propyl groups on the nitrogen. This N carries only one carbon group and two H.

q: Which condensed formula is tert-butylamine?
h: A tert-butyl group is attached through a carbon that bears three methyl groups.
w: tert-Butyl is (CH3)3C–, so tert-butylamine is (CH3)3CNH2. The others are sec-butylamine, butylamine and isobutylamine.
x: This is sec-butylamine: the N is on a carbon bonded to two other carbons. A tert-butyl carbon is bonded to three CH<sub>3</sub> groups.
This is butylamine: a straight chain with N on the end carbon. The tert-butyl group is highly branched.
This is isobutylamine: the N is on a CH<sub>2</sub> next to the branch. In tert-butyl, the N carbon itself carries the branches.

q: Methylamine is a weak base. Which ions form when it dissolves in water?
h: The lone pair on nitrogen accepts an H<sup>+</sup> from water.
w: CH3NH2 + H2O ⇌ CH3NH+3 + OH−. The amine is the proton acceptor, so hydroxide ions form and the solution is basic.
x: An amine acts as a base, so its nitrogen gains an H<sup>+</sup>; it does not lose one. Producing H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> would make it an acid.
Dissolving in water does not break the C–N bond. The amine stays intact and only its nitrogen lone pair reacts.
If the amine takes H<sup>+</sup> from water, what is left of the water molecule? It cannot also form H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>.

q: Many amine drugs, such as diphenhydramine, are sold as hydrochloride salts. Why?
c: The ionic salt is more soluble in water and body fluids.
The salt is a stronger base than the free amine.
The salt is more volatile, so it is absorbed faster.
HCl converts the amine into a more stable amide.
h: What happens to an amine's nitrogen when it reacts with HCl?
w: Amine + HCl → ammonium chloride salt. The ionic salt dissolves well in water and is a stable, odorless solid. It is not an amide, and salts are less volatile, not more.
x: The salt is the protonated (conjugate acid) form, so it is no longer a base at all. Its advantage is about how it behaves in water.
Ionic salts are less volatile than free amines; they are odorless solids. Think about what ionic compounds do in water.
HCl just transfers H<sup>+</sup> to the N, making an ammonium salt. Forming an amide would require a carboxylic acid and heat.

q: Which isomer of C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>9</sub>N has the lowest boiling point?
h: Which amine has no N–H bond for hydrogen bonding between its molecules?
w: A 3° amine has no H on nitrogen, so it cannot H-bond to itself; trimethylamine boils at only ~3 °C. The 1° and 2° isomers have N–H bonds, so they hydrogen bond and boil higher (about 32–48 °C).
x: Propylamine is a 1° amine with two N–H bonds, so its molecules hydrogen bond to each other. That raises its boiling point (about 48 °C).
Ethylmethylamine is a 2° amine; its N–H still lets molecules hydrogen bond to each other, raising the boiling point.
Isopropylamine is a 1° amine with two N–H bonds, so it can hydrogen bond to itself. Look for the isomer with no N–H.

q: Propanoic acid is heated with methylamine. What is the organic product of this amidation?
h: The –OH of the acid and an H from the amine leave as water; N attaches to the C=O carbon.
w: CH3CH2COOH + H2NCH3 → CH3CH2CONHCH3 + H2O: N-methylpropanamide. Methyl propanoate would come from methanol, not methylamine.
x: That name puts the C=O on a one-carbon (methanoic) piece and a propyl on N, which swaps the two parts. The C=O stays with the acid's three-carbon chain.
An ester like methyl propanoate forms from an acid and an alcohol (methanol). Here the partner is an amine, so the new bond is C–N.
An amine has no C=O, but the acid's carbonyl stays in the product. Amidation keeps the C=O and forms a new C–N bond.

q: N-Ethylethanamide, CH<sub>3</sub>CONHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, is heated with aqueous NaOH. What are the products?
h: Base hydrolysis of an amide gives the carboxylate salt and the free amine.
w: Hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond; in NaOH the acid becomes sodium ethanoate and the N part is released as ethylamine. Acid hydrolysis would instead give the free acid and the ammonium salt; ammonia would come only from an unsubstituted amide.
x: These are acid hydrolysis products. In NaOH the acid cannot stay neutral and the amine cannot stay protonated.
Hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond of the amide, not a bond elsewhere. No alcohol forms, and the C=O carbon cannot keep its N.
Ammonia comes only from an amide with an unsubstituted –NH<sub>2</sub>. Here the N carries an ethyl group, which stays attached when it is released.

q: Nicotine, caffeine and morphine are physiologically active nitrogen-containing compounds from plants. They are called
h: The name hints that these compounds are basic, like alkalis.
w: Plant-derived, biologically active amines are alkaloids. Many medicines (codeine, quinine, atropine) come from this group.
x: Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins, with both –NH<sub>2</sub> and –COOH groups. These plant compounds are a different, basic group.
Steroids are lipids built on a four-ring carbon skeleton, often with no nitrogen. These compounds are defined by their basic nitrogen.
Terpenes are plant compounds built from isoprene units and usually contain no nitrogen. The key feature here is a basic N.

q: Nylon 6,6, used in sutures, is a polyamide made from hexanedioic acid and 1,6-hexanediamine. What linkage joins the monomers?
h: A carboxylic acid reacting with an amine forms which bond?
w: Each –COOH reacts with an –NH2 to form an amide bond, releasing water; that is why nylon is a polyamide. Polyesters such as PET use ester linkages.
x: An ester linkage forms from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol. Nylon's monomers are an acid and an amine, which react differently.
An ether linkage is C–O–C with no C=O, formed between alcohols. Neither monomer here reacts that way.
Glycosidic bonds link sugar units in carbohydrates. Nylon is made from a dicarboxylic acid and a diamine, not sugars.

q: Choline, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>N<sup>+</sup>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH, is needed to make the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. How is its nitrogen classified?
h: Count the carbon atoms bonded directly to nitrogen.
w: Nitrogen is bonded to four carbons (three CH3 and one CH2) and carries a + charge: quaternary ammonium ion. A tertiary amine has only three carbons on a neutral N.
x: A tertiary amine has three carbons on a neutral N. Count again: choline's N carries a CH<sub>2</sub> as well as three CH<sub>3</sub>, and it has a + charge.
A secondary amine has two carbons and one H on N. Choline's nitrogen has no H at all.
A primary amine has only one carbon on N. Count every carbon bonded to choline's nitrogen.

q: Acetaminophen is an amide, HO–C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>–NH–C(=O)–CH<sub>3</sub>. Which carboxylic acid and amine could form it by condensation?
h: The C=O side of an amide came from the carboxylic acid; the N side came from the amine.
w: The C(=O)CH3 piece is from acetic acid, and the HO–C6H4–NH– piece is from the amine 4-aminophenol: acetic acid and 4-aminophenol. 4-Hydroxybenzoic acid + methylamine would put the C=O on the ring side, a different compound.
x: Pairing 4-hydroxybenzoic acid with methylamine puts the C=O on the ring side and the CH<sub>3</sub> on N, a different compound. Check which side of the N the C=O is on.
Phenol has no nitrogen, so it cannot supply the N–H needed for an amide. The ring piece must come from an amine.
Formic acid supplies only an H–C=O piece. In acetaminophen the C=O carbon also carries a CH<sub>3</sub>.

q: How is tetramethylammonium chloride, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>N<sup>+</sup> Cl<sup>−</sup>, classified?
h: Count the carbon groups bonded to nitrogen. What happens when there are four?
w: Nitrogen has four C–N bonds, no N–H and a + charge, so this is a quaternary ammonium salt. A tertiary amine has three carbon groups and a neutral N; its salt, R3NH+, still has an N–H.
x: A tertiary ammonium salt is a protonated 3° amine, R<sub>3</sub>NH<sup>+</sup>, which still has an N–H. This nitrogen has no H.
A tertiary amine has three carbons on a neutral N. This N has more carbon groups and carries a + charge.
A primary amine salt is RNH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, with just one carbon on N. Count the CH<sub>3</sub> groups on this nitrogen.

q: Methamphetamine is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)NHCH<sub>3</sub>. Its amine group is classified as
h: For amines, count carbons bonded directly to the N, not to the carbon next to it.
w: The N is bonded to two carbons (the CH and the CH3) and one H: secondary (2°). Calling it 1° comes from using the alcohol rule (looking at the carbon) instead of counting carbons on N.
x: That comes from counting carbons on the neighboring carbon, the alcohol rule. For amines, count carbons bonded directly to N: here CH and CH<sub>3</sub>.
A tertiary amine has three carbons on N and no N–H. Methamphetamine's N still has one H.
A quaternary ammonium ion has four carbons on a positively charged N. This N is neutral and bears an H.

q: How would you name CH<sub>3</sub>NHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, a secondary amine, using common (alkyl + amine) naming?
h: Name each alkyl group attached to N, in alphabetical order, then add "amine".
w: The N carries one ethyl and one methyl group: ethylmethylamine, a 2° amine. Propylamine has all three carbons in one chain, and an "-amide" would need a C=O on the N.
x: Propylamine has all three carbons in one chain on N. Here the N sits between a CH<sub>3</sub> and a CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, two separate groups.
Diethylamine has two ethyl groups on N, four carbons in all. This compound has only three carbons.
An amide name needs a C=O carbon bonded to N. CH<sub>3</sub>NHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> has no carbonyl group.

q: Dimethylamine, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>NH, and acetic acid are heated together and water is driven off. Which amide forms?
h: Remove –OH from the acid and the H from the N. The amine keeps both of its other groups.
w: The acid's –OH and the N–H combine as H2O and the new C–N bond joins CH3CO– to –N(CH3)2: CH3CON(CH3)2, N,N-dimethylethanamide. CH3CONHCH3 loses one of the amine's methyl groups.
x: CH<sub>3</sub>CONHCH<sub>3</sub> has only one methyl on N. Dimethylamine loses only its H in amidation, so both methyl groups stay.
This structure has no C=O, so it is an amine, not an amide. Amidation keeps the acid's carbonyl group.
HCON(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> has an H on the C=O carbon, so it comes from formic acid. Acetic acid supplies CH<sub>3</sub>CO–.

q: When ethylamine, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, is mixed with hydrochloric acid, which substance is formed?
h: Amines are organic bases. What does a base do with the H<sup>+</sup> from an acid?
w: The lone pair on N accepts H+ from HCl, giving the salt CH3CH2NH+3 Cl− (ethylammonium chloride). Nothing is substituted; it is a simple acid–base (neutralization) reaction.
x: No bond to carbon is broken; the C–N bond stays intact. An amine is a base, so think about what the N does with H<sup>+</sup>.
HCl does not attach Cl to nitrogen or release H<sub>2</sub>. This is a simple acid–base reaction.
An amine is a base, so its N gains H<sup>+</sup> rather than losing it. Forming H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> would make the amine act as an acid.

q: Hot aqueous HCl hydrolyzes propanamide, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub>. Which products result?
h: Hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond. In acid, what happens to the nitrogen piece that is released?
w: Water splits the C–N bond: the C=O side becomes CH3CH2COOH and the N side is NH3, which picks up H+ in acid: propanoic acid and NH4Cl. A sodium salt plus NH3 is what forms in NaOH instead.
x: Sodium propanoate and NH<sub>3</sub> form in NaOH (basic hydrolysis). Here the solution is acidic HCl.
Hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond but leaves the C=O in place. An alcohol would need the carbonyl to be reduced.
Propanamine has no C=O, and hydrolysis adds water rather than producing it. The amide C–N bond is what breaks.

q: Name the amide CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CONHCH<sub>3</sub> using IUPAC rules.
h: The chain that includes the C=O carbon is the parent. Groups on the nitrogen get the prefix N-.
w: The C=O chain, CH3CH2CH2CH2CO–, has 5 carbons (pentanamide) and the CH3 on N is named N-methyl: N-methylpentanamide. Counting the N–CH3 into the chain gives the wrong "hexanamide"; "-amine" ignores the C=O.
x: Hexanamide counts the N–CH<sub>3</sub> carbon as part of the chain. The parent chain includes only the carbons on the C=O side.
That name puts a five-carbon group on N and a one-carbon C=O piece. Here the C=O is at the end of the five-carbon chain, with CH<sub>3</sub> on N.
The -amine ending ignores the C=O bonded to the nitrogen. An N attached to a carbonyl carbon makes this an amide.

q: Which compound will NOT form an amide when heated with acetic acid?
h: Amidation needs to remove an H from the nitrogen to make water. Which nitrogen has no H?
w: Forming the amide removes –OH from the acid and an H from N. (CH3)3N, a 3° amine, has no N–H, so it can only form a salt with the acid, not an amide. NH3, 1° and 2° amines all have N–H.
x: Dimethylamine still has one N–H, which can leave with the acid's –OH as water. It can form an amide.
Methylamine has two N–H bonds, so it can lose one H as water and form an amide.
NH<sub>3</sub> has three N–H bonds and forms a simple amide with acetic acid on heating.

q: Fish smells "fishy" partly because of volatile amines such as trimethylamine. Squeezing lemon juice on fish reduces the odor mainly because
c: the acid converts the amines into nonvolatile ammonium salts
the acid converts the amines into amides
the acid oxidizes the amines to carboxylic acids
the acid converts the amines into esters
h: Amines are organic bases; lemon juice contains citric acid. What forms when an acid and a base react?
w: Citric acid donates H+ to the amine N, forming an ammonium salt. The ionic salt is water-soluble and not volatile, so it does not reach your nose. Amides would require heating, and a 3° amine cannot form one.
x: Making an amide requires heating with water driven off, not a squeeze of lemon. Trimethylamine also has no N–H, so it cannot form one.
Citric acid is not an oxidizing agent, and amines do not oxidize to carboxylic acids. Think acid plus base.
Esters form from carboxylic acids and alcohols. Amines are bases, so what does an acid do to them?

q: Propanoic acid and methylamine, shown, are heated together so that water is removed. What is the organic product?
h: Amidation: –OH from the acid and H from the amine leave as water; the C=O stays with the acid part.
w: The acid carbonyl carbon bonds to the N of methylamine, giving N-methylpropanamide. N-Ethylacetamide has the C=O on the wrong side; the amine has lost the C=O; the methyl ester would come from methanol, not methylamine.
x: This drawing is N-ethylacetamide: the C=O is on a two-carbon piece and an ethyl is on N. The acid's C=O must stay with its three-carbon chain.
This drawing is an amine (N-methylpropylamine) with no C=O. Amidation keeps the acid's carbonyl oxygen.
This drawing is an ester, methyl propanoate, with an O between the C=O and the CH<sub>3</sub>. An ester would need methanol; methylamine gives a C–N bond.

q: N-Ethylacetamide, shown, is heated with water and HCl (acid hydrolysis). What are the products?
h: Hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond of the amide. In acid, what happens to the amine that forms?
w: Water breaks the amide C–N bond, giving acetic acid and ethylamine; in HCl the amine is protonated, so the products are acetic acid + ethylammonium chloride. "Ethylamine" ignores that the solution is acidic; acetamide + ethanol breaks the wrong bond (N–Cethyl).
x: This shows neutral ethylamine, but the reaction runs in HCl. An amine in acid picks up H<sup>+</sup>.
This drawing breaks the N–ethyl bond, giving acetamide and ethanol. Hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond next to the C=O.
This shows acetate ion, which cannot survive in HCl; it would be protonated. There is also no chloride ion to balance the ammonium charge.

q: Trimethylamine gives spoiled fish its odor. It reacts with HCl as shown. What is the product?
h: Amines are bases: the lone pair on N picks up H<sup>+</sup> from the acid.
w: The N lone pair accepts H+, giving the ammonium ion (CH3)3NH+ with Cl−: trimethylammonium chloride, an odorless, water-soluble salt (why lemon juice helps with fish odor). No new C–Cl or N–Cl bond forms, and no methyl group is added (that would be a quaternary ammonium salt).
x: This drawing has four CH<sub>3</sub> groups on N, a quaternary ammonium salt. HCl adds only H<sup>+</sup> to the nitrogen, not a methyl group.
This drawing puts Cl on a carbon (CH<sub>2</sub>Cl). HCl does not make C–Cl bonds with an amine; it is an acid–base reaction.
This drawing bonds Cl directly to N. The nitrogen lone pair picks up H<sup>+</sup>, and chloride stays a separate ion.

q: Pseudoephedrine, shown, is a nasal decongestant. How are its alcohol group and its amine group classified?
h: For the alcohol, count carbons on the C–OH carbon. For the amine, count carbons bonded directly to N.
w: The C–OH carbon is bonded to the ring carbon and to the CH(CH3) carbon: a 2° alcohol. The N is bonded to two carbons (CH3 and the chain CH) and one H: a 2° amine. For amines, count the carbons on the N itself, not on a neighboring carbon.
x: The C–OH carbon is bonded to two carbons: the ring carbon and the CH(CH<sub>3</sub>) carbon. Count them again for the alcohol.
The N is bonded to two carbons (a CH<sub>3</sub> and the chain CH) plus one H. Count carbons on the nitrogen itself.
The C–OH carbon still has an H, and the N still has an H. Neither group has three carbons attached.

q: Amphetamine, a stimulant used to treat ADHD, is shown. How is the nitrogen labeled a classified?
h: For amines, count the carbon atoms bonded directly to the nitrogen, not to the carbon that holds it.
w: The N is bonded to only one carbon (plus two H), so amphetamine is a primary (1°) amine. Calling it 2° uses the alcohol rule (the carbon holding the group is bonded to two carbons); amines are classified by the N itself.
x: That uses the alcohol rule: the carbon holding the N has two carbon neighbors. For amines, count carbons bonded directly to N.
A tertiary amine has three carbons on N and no N–H. Nitrogen a is –NH<sub>2</sub>.
A quaternary ammonium ion has four carbons on a positive N. Nitrogen a is neutral and carries two H.

q: Diphenhydramine, the antihistamine in Benadryl, is shown. How is the nitrogen labeled a classified?
h: Count the carbons bonded directly to N. In a line drawing, each line from N that ends without a letter is a CH<sub>3</sub>.
w: The N has three bonds to carbon (two CH3 line ends and the CH2 of the chain) and no H: a tertiary (3°) amine. Students who count only the chain carbon miss the two methyl line ends; a quaternary ion would need four carbons and a + charge.
x: A secondary amine has an N–H. Nitrogen a has no H; remember each line ending at N without a label is a CH<sub>3</sub>.
A primary amine has an –NH<sub>2</sub> with one carbon. Count the CH<sub>3</sub> line ends on nitrogen a as well as the chain carbon.
A quaternary ammonium ion has four carbons and a + charge on N. Nitrogen a is neutral.

q: Lidocaine, a local anesthetic, has two nitrogen atoms, a and b. Which statement is correct?
c: a is a 3° amine; b is part of an amide
a is a 3° amine; b is a 2° amine
a is a 2° amine; b is part of an amide
a is part of an amide; b is a 1° amine
h: An N bonded to a C=O carbon belongs to an amide, not an amine. For the other N, count the attached carbons.
w: N a is bonded to three carbons (two ethyls and a CH2): a 3° amine. N b is bonded to the C=O carbon, so it is part of an amide. Calling b a 2° amine counts its two carbons but misses the C=O, which makes it an amide (much less basic).
x: N b is bonded to a C=O carbon. An N attached to a carbonyl carbon belongs to an amide, not an amine.
N a has two ethyl groups and a CH<sub>2</sub>: count every carbon on it, including both ethyls.
N a is not bonded to the C=O carbon; a CH<sub>2</sub> sits between them. N b is bonded to the C=O and to the ring, so it is not an –NH<sub>2</sub>.

q: Nicotine is shown. How is the nitrogen labeled a, in the five-membered ring, classified?
h: Ring carbons count too. Count every carbon bonded directly to nitrogen a, including the CH<sub>3</sub> line end.
w: N a is bonded to two ring carbons and the CH3, with no H: a tertiary (3°) amine. Choosing 2° counts only the two ring bonds and forgets the methyl line end.
x: That counts only the two ring bonds. The line from nitrogen a ending with no label is a CH<sub>3</sub>, a third carbon.
A primary amine has an –NH<sub>2</sub>. Nitrogen a has no H; it is bonded to ring carbons and a CH<sub>3</sub>.
A quaternary ammonium ion needs four carbons and a + charge on N. Nitrogen a is neutral.

q: Which of these drugs or neurotransmitters is a secondary (2°) amine?
h: A 2° amine N is bonded to two carbons and one H, and neither carbon is a C=O carbon.
w: Methamphetamine has an N–H with a CH3 and a chain carbon on N: 2°. Acetaminophen also has an N bonded to two carbons and one H, but one of those carbons is a C=O, so it is an amide, not an amine. Dopamine is 1°, and nicotine (both N have no H) is not 2°.
x: This is dopamine: its N is an –NH<sub>2</sub> on the end of a chain, bonded to only one carbon.
This is acetaminophen: its N–H nitrogen is bonded to a C=O carbon, which makes it part of an amide, not an amine.
This is nicotine: neither nitrogen has an H. The ring N with the CH<sub>3</sub> is bonded to three carbons.

q: Which structure contains a quaternary ammonium ion?
h: Quaternary means four carbons on the nitrogen. A + charge alone is not enough.
w: Acetylcholine, the neurotransmitter at nerve–muscle junctions, has N+ bonded to four carbons (three CH3 and a CH2). Protonated methamphetamine (the form in its hydrochloride salt) is also positive, but its N+ has only two carbons and two H: it is just a protonated 2° amine. Dopamine and lidocaine are neutral amines.
x: This N is positive, but it carries two H and only two carbons: it is just a protonated 2° amine. Quaternary needs four carbons on N.
This is dopamine, with a neutral –NH<sub>2</sub>. It has only one carbon on N and no charge.
This is lidocaine: its amine N has three carbons and no charge, and the other N is part of an amide.

q: The four amines shown are isomers, C4H11N. Which one cannot hydrogen bond to other molecules of itself?
h: Classify each amine: 1°, 2° or 3°. Which kind has no H on the nitrogen?
w: The 3° amine (N,N-dimethylethylamine) has three carbons on N and no N–H, so it cannot donate a hydrogen bond to another molecule of itself. The 1° amine (two N–H) and the 2° amines (one N–H) can. A 3° amine still accepts hydrogen bonds from water through its N lone pair.
x: This is butylamine, a 1° amine with two N–H bonds, so its molecules can hydrogen bond to each other.
This is a 2° amine (N-methylpropylamine). Its one N–H lets molecules hydrogen bond to each other.
This is diethylamine, a 2° amine with one N–H, so it can hydrogen bond to itself.

q: Butanoic acid and ethylamine are heated together and water is driven off. What is the organic product of the reaction shown?
h: Amidation: the acid loses –OH and the amine loses an H from N; the new C–N bond makes an amide.
w: The acid C=O carbon bonds to the N of ethylamine: N-ethylbutanamide + H2O. N-Butylacetamide is an isomer with the C=O on the wrong side of the N. The ammonium carboxylate salt forms when the two are just mixed (acid–base), but heating drives off water to make the amide. The amine has lost the C=O oxygen.
x: This drawing is N-butylacetamide: the C=O is on a two-carbon piece with a butyl on N. The acid's C=O must stay with its four-carbon chain.
This ammonium carboxylate salt forms when the two are simply mixed. Heating with water driven off gives a different product.
This drawing is an amine with no C=O. Amidation keeps the acid's carbonyl oxygen.

q: Nicotinic acid (niacin, vitamin B<sub>3</sub>) is heated with NH<sub>3</sub> and water is removed, as shown. The product is another form of vitamin B<sub>3</sub>. What is it?
h: NH<sub>3</sub> replaces the –OH of the carboxylic acid group. The ring is unchanged.
w: The –COOH loses –OH, NH3 loses an H, and a C–N bond forms: nicotinamide (–CONH2). Ammonium nicotinate is only the acid–base salt, which loses water on heating to form the amide. The other two have lost the C=O oxygen or the whole carbonyl carbon.
x: This is ammonium nicotinate, the acid–base salt. Heating removes water and forms a new bond instead.
This drawing has lost the whole carbonyl carbon: the N is bonded straight to the ring. Amidation keeps the C=O carbon.
This drawing has a CH<sub>2</sub> where the C=O should be; the carbonyl oxygen is gone. Amidation keeps the C=O.

q: Acetanilide was one of the first fever reducers. What are the products of the reaction shown?
h: Hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond next to the C=O. In acid, what happens to the amine that forms?
w: Water breaks the amide C–N bond, giving acetic acid and aniline; in HCl the amine picks up H+, so the products are acetic acid + anilinium chloride. Neutral aniline ignores the acid present. Acetamide + phenol breaks the N–ring bond instead of the amide bond, and sodium acetate forms only in NaOH.
x: This shows neutral aniline, but the reaction runs in HCl. An amine in acid picks up H<sup>+</sup>.
This drawing breaks the N–ring bond, giving acetamide and phenol. Hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond next to the C=O.
Sodium acetate forms only in NaOH. With HCl as the reagent, no sodium is present.

q: DEET is the active ingredient in many insect repellents. What are the products of the reaction shown?
h: Base hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond next to the C=O. In base, the acid part is a salt and the amine is neutral.
w: OH− breaks the amide C–N bond: the carbonyl side becomes sodium 3-methylbenzoate and the N side becomes diethylamine. In base the carboxylic acid cannot stay neutral, and the amine cannot be protonated (no Na+ appears in the ammonium salt choice). Breaking an N–ethyl bond (giving ethanol) does not hydrolyze the amide group.
x: An ammonium ion like this cannot exist in strong base; OH<sup>−</sup> removes its H<sup>+</sup>. There is also no Na<sup>+</sup> to pair with the carboxylate.
This shows a neutral carboxylic acid, which cannot survive in NaOH. In base the acid is converted to its salt.
This drawing breaks an N–ethyl bond, giving an N-ethyl amide and ethanol. Hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond next to the C=O.

q: What are the products of the reaction of N-ethylbenzamide shown?
h: In acid, the carbonyl side becomes a carboxylic acid and the nitrogen side picks up H<sup>+</sup>.
w: Water breaks the C–N bond next to the C=O: benzoic acid + ethylammonium chloride (the ethylamine is protonated by HCl). Neutral ethylamine ignores the acid. Benzamide + ethanol breaks the N–ethyl bond instead, and sodium benzoate + ethylamine are the products in NaOH.
x: This shows neutral ethylamine, but the reaction runs in HCl. An amine in acid picks up H<sup>+</sup>.
This drawing breaks the N–ethyl bond, giving benzamide and ethanol. Hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond next to the C=O.
Sodium benzoate forms only in NaOH. With HCl as the reagent, no sodium is present.

q: Amphetamine, a prescription stimulant, is sold as a salt made by the reaction shown. What is the product?
h: Amines are bases. Only the N changes: –NH2 picks up H+ and becomes –NH+3.
w: The lone pair on N accepts H+ from HCl, giving the ammonium ion with Cl−: amphetamine hydrochloride, a water-soluble salt. No C–Cl or N–Cl bond forms: Cl replacing –NH2, Cl on the ring, or Cl on N are all wrong.
x: This drawing has Cl replacing the –NH<sub>2</sub>. HCl does not swap out the nitrogen; it is an acid–base reaction.
This drawing puts Cl on the benzene ring and leaves the –NH<sub>2</sub> unchanged. HCl reacts with the basic N, not the ring.
This drawing has an N–Cl bond. The nitrogen lone pair picks up H<sup>+</sup>, and chloride stays a separate ion.

q: What is the product of the reaction of ethylenediamine (1,2-ethanediamine) shown?
h: Each amine group is a base. With excess acid, how many N atoms are protonated?
w: Both –NH2 groups accept H+, so with excess HCl the product is ethylenediammonium chloride, with two –NH+3 groups and two Cl− ions. Protonating only one N would be the product with just one HCl. HCl does not make N–Cl or C–Cl bonds.
x: This protonates only one –NH<sub>2</sub>, which is what one equivalent of HCl would do. With excess acid, check the other nitrogen too.
This drawing bonds Cl to each N. HCl gives H<sup>+</sup> to the nitrogen; chloride stays a separate ion.
This drawing replaces an –NH<sub>2</sub> with Cl and releases NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>. HCl does not break C–N bonds; it is an acid–base reaction.

q: Which carboxylic acid and amine, heated together, form the amide shown?
h: Break the C–N bond next to the C=O. The C=O side is the acid; the N side is the amine.
w: The C=O side, CH3CH2C(=O)–, comes from propanoic acid, and the N bonded to the middle carbon of a three-carbon group comes from isopropylamine. 2-Methylpropanoic acid + ethylamine gives an isomer with the C=O on the other side. 2-Propanol gives an ester, not an amide, and propylamine attaches N to an end carbon.
x: 2-Methylpropanoic acid + ethylamine makes an isomer with the branch on the C=O side and ethyl on N. In the target, the C=O side is an unbranched ethyl.
2-Propanol is an alcohol, so heating it with an acid gives an ester, not an amide. An amide needs an amine.
Propylamine would put the N on an end carbon. In the drawing the N is bonded to the middle carbon of a branched three-carbon group.

q: Phenylacetic acid and dimethylamine are heated together and water is removed. What is the organic product of the reaction shown?
h: Replace the –OH of the acid with the N of the amine, keeping both methyl groups on N.
w: The acid C=O carbon bonds to the N of dimethylamine and H2O is lost: N,N-dimethyl-2-phenylacetamide. The dimethylammonium salt is the acid–base product before heating removes water. The amine has lost the C=O oxygen, and N,N-dimethylbenzamide is missing the CH2 between the ring and the C=O.
x: This dimethylammonium carboxylate salt is the acid–base product of simply mixing. Heating drives off water and forms a new bond.
This drawing has a CH<sub>2</sub> where the C=O should be, so it is an amine. Amidation keeps the acid's carbonyl oxygen.
This drawing has the C=O bonded directly to the ring, missing the CH<sub>2</sub> of phenylacetic acid. That would come from benzoic acid.

q: What are the products of the reaction of benzamide shown?
h: Base hydrolysis: the carbonyl side becomes a carboxylate salt and the nitrogen comes off as NH<sub>3</sub>.
w: OH− breaks the C–N bond: sodium benzoate + NH3. Benzoic acid + NH4Cl are the products in HCl, not NaOH. In base the acid cannot stay neutral, and NH+4 cannot exist in strong base (it gives up H+ to OH−).
x: Benzoic acid and NH<sub>4</sub>Cl are the products of acid hydrolysis with HCl. Here the reagent is NaOH.
This shows a neutral carboxylic acid, which cannot survive in NaOH; the base converts it to its salt.
NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> cannot exist in strong base: it gives its H<sup>+</sup> to OH<sup>−</sup>. Also, no Na<sup>+</sup> is shown to balance the charge.

q: Which compound acts as a base in water, raising the pH of the solution?
h: A base accepts a proton. Which atom here has a lone pair that readily picks up H<sup>+</sup> from water?
w: The nitrogen of cyclohexylamine accepts H+ from water, leaving OH− behind and raising the pH: amines are the organic bases. The carboxylic acid lowers the pH; the alcohol and the ketone are neutral, since their oxygens do not take protons from water to any useful extent.
x: This is a carboxylic acid: it donates H<sup>+</sup> to water and lowers the pH.
This is an alcohol, cyclohexanol. Its oxygen does not take protons from water to any useful extent, so the solution stays neutral.
This is a ketone, cyclohexanone. Its oxygen does not take protons from water to a useful extent, so it is neutral.

q: Propanoic acid and ethylamine are simply mixed at room temperature; nothing is heated. Which pair of products forms?
h: Acid + base at room temperature is a proton transfer, not a condensation. The acid gives H<sup>+</sup>; the amine takes it.
w: The carboxylic acid donates H+ to the amine nitrogen, giving the propanoate ion and the ethylammonium ion (a salt). The amide forms only when the mixture is heated so water is driven off. Propanoate paired with a neutral amine is unbalanced: the proton must land on the N. The ester would require an alcohol, not an amine.
x: This amide forms only when the mixture is heated and water is driven off. At room temperature there is just a fast proton transfer.
This shows the acid losing H<sup>+</sup>, but the H<sup>+</sup> has to go somewhere. The amine is the base that takes it.
This is an ester, ethyl propanoate, which needs an alcohol. Ethylamine is an amine, not an alcohol.

q: Exactly one of the drawn nitrogen compounds is a tertiary (3°) amine. Which one?
h: Count the carbons bonded directly to N, and make sure the N is not attached to a C=O.
w: In N-methylpiperidine the nitrogen is bonded to three carbons (two ring carbons and the CH3) and to no C=O: a 3° amine. Piperidine (N–H, two ring carbons) is a 2° amine and cyclohexylamine (NH2) is 1°. N,N-dimethylacetamide also has three carbons on N, but one of them is a C=O carbon, which makes it an amide, not an amine.
x: This is piperidine: its N has an H and only two ring carbons, so it is a 2° amine.
This is cyclohexylamine: its N is an –NH<sub>2</sub> with one carbon, so it is a 1° amine.
This N has three carbons, but one of them is a C=O carbon. An N bonded to a carbonyl carbon is an amide, not an amine.

q: Pyrrolidine, a cyclic secondary amine, condenses with acetic acid on heating (water is lost). Which drawing is the amide formed?
h: Acid –OH plus amine N–H leave as water; the new bond is C(=O)–N. A 2° amine gives an amide with no N–H.
w: The acid's –OH and the amine's only N–H are lost as water, joining the C=O carbon to the ring nitrogen: N-acetylpyrrolidine, an amide whose N carries two ring carbons and the acetyl group. The N-cyclopentyl amide has the N outside the ring (that would require cyclopentylamine). The ammonium acetate ion pair is what forms without heating. The structure with a C–OH in place of the C=O is not an amide: amidation keeps the acid's C=O and removes its –OH.
x: This drawing puts the N–H outside the ring on a cyclopentyl group; that would need cyclopentylamine. Pyrrolidine's N is part of the ring.
This acetate and pyrrolidinium ion pair is the acid–base salt that forms without heating. Heating drives off water and forms a new bond.
This drawing has a C–OH where the carbonyl should be. Amidation keeps the acid's C=O and removes its –OH.

q: Which statement best describes a neurotransmitter?
c: a chemical messenger released by a nerve cell that crosses a synapse and binds to receptors on the next cell
a hormone carried by the blood to organs far from where it is made
an enzyme that breaks down nerve signals in the brain
the electrical signal that travels along a nerve fiber
h: Think about how a signal gets across the tiny gap between two nerve cells.
w: A neurotransmitter is a chemical messenger released by a nerve cell. It crosses the synapse, binds to receptors on the next cell, and is then removed or broken down. Many neurotransmitters are amines, such as dopamine and serotonin.
x: A hormone travels through the blood to distant tissues. A neurotransmitter acts across the short gap between two cells.
Enzymes such as acetylcholinesterase break neurotransmitters down, but the enzyme is not the messenger itself.
The electrical signal travels along the nerve fiber. At the synapse a chemical messenger carries the signal to the next cell.

q: Dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin and histamine are all neurotransmitters. Which functional group do all four contain, which is protonated (–NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>) at body pH?
h: These compounds are made from amino acids by removing the –COOH group. Which group is left?
w: All four contain an amine group. Like other amines, it is a weak base and is mostly protonated in body fluids, so these neurotransmitters carry a positive charge.
x: An amide has N bonded to a C=O. These neurotransmitters have N bonded only to carbon and hydrogen atoms.
These compounds are made by removing the –COOH group from an amino acid, so they have no carboxylic acid left.
An ester is a C=O bonded to an –OR group. Acetylcholine is an ester, but these four neurotransmitters are amines.

q: SSRI antidepressants such as fluoxetine (Prozac) block the reuptake of serotonin, the step in which the sending nerve cell takes serotonin back in from the synapse. What is the effect?
c: Serotonin stays in the synapse longer, so its signal to the next cell lasts longer
Serotonin is broken down faster in the synapse
Serotonin can no longer bind to its receptors
h: If the sending cell cannot take serotonin back in, where does the serotonin stay?
w: Reuptake normally clears serotonin from the synapse and ends its signal. Blocking it means serotonin stays in the synapse longer and keeps acting on the receptors of the next cell.
x: An SSRI acts on the reuptake protein. It does not stop the body from making serotonin.
Blocking reuptake leaves more serotonin in the synapse, not less. Faster breakdown would weaken the signal.
That would describe a receptor blocker. SSRIs leave the receptors free, and more serotonin is available to bind them.

q: Ammonia (NH<sub>3</sub>) from dairies and fertilizer reacts in Valley air with nitric acid (HNO<sub>3</sub>) from vehicle exhaust, forming tiny particles of ammonium nitrate, NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub>. In this reaction, ammonia acts as
c: a base that accepts H<sup>+</sup> to form the ammonium ion
a catalyst that is not changed
h: Amines and ammonia have a lone pair on nitrogen. What do they do with H<sup>+</sup>?
w: Like an amine, ammonia uses its nitrogen lone pair to accept H+ from the acid, forming NH4+. The product, ammonium nitrate, is an ammonium salt, just like the salt formed when an amine reacts with HCl.
x: Nitric acid donates the H<sup>+</sup>. Ammonia gains it.
This is an acid–base reaction. No electrons are transferred between the reactants.
Ammonia is used up and becomes part of the product, so it is not a catalyst.
